text.p: As the world's oldest national park celebrates its 125th anniversary on March 1, park officials said they were looking at the past and the present to plot a course for its future.
"We are able to celebrate Yellowstone's anniversary because of the vision of those who preceded us 125 years ago," park Superintendent Mike Finely said.

"How we meet the challenges today will determine what we as a people will celebrate 125 years from now," he said, adding that they would need equal doses of vision and wisdom to make sure the beautiful, unusual park survives intact for future generations.

The challenges are many, he said. Funding is so short rangers often spend more time directing traffic than explaining the park's wonders. Critics in Congress are investigating Park Service management practices and bison are slaughtered by the hundreds at the park's boundaries. Fires swept through half the park in 1988 and newly reintroduced wolves still agitate neighbouring ranchers.

Yet the park remains very popular. After all, there are not many places in the world where people can see wild bison, grizzly bears and geysers all in the same day, rangers said. The park hosts more than three million visitors annually from all over the world, so many managers have considered limiting the numbers lest the park be overrun and its natural resources destroyed.

Celebrations will go on all year to commemorate the March 1, 1872, law signed by President Ulysses S. Grant that set aside Yellowstone's 2.2 million acres (890,300 hectares) "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people."

"The best idea America ever had," Finley said. The creation of Yellowstone grew into a system incorporating 374 parks, monuments and preserves across the nation that celebrate America's history, culture and natural wonders.
More than 140 other countries have used the U.S. model to set up their own national parks.

Tourists arrive in Yellowstone today in cars and vans and are faced with traffic jams and potholes, but the earliest visitors braved other conditions. In addition to wildlife, visitors in the late 1800s also stumbled on Indian skirmishes and holdups by stagecoach bandits.

Throughout its history, Yellowstone managers have laboured under an often conflicting mandate -- to protect the park's natural resources and to provide a way for people to enjoy them. In the past they built roads and hotels for tourists, but now the focus is on preservation, Secretary of the Interior Bruce Babbitt, who oversees the park system, told a conference in 1994.

Nevertheless, Yellowstone and other parks remain powerful economic engines for surrounding communities, bringing in tourist dollars. In the 1995 U.S. budget dispute, visitors were incensed when the federal government closed the parks.
